subproblem.title: Jacobian identity for the slice map: J_m(A∘D∘ι) = |γ|·J_n(A)·|det D| in Gram-determinant form
subproblem.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ, n := m+1, A : ℝⁿ → ℝ^P and D : ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ continuous linear maps, and γ ∈ ℝ^P with γ ∈ range A and ⟨γ, A(D y)⟩ = y_0 for every y ∈ ℝⁿ. With e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1, √det(⟨A D e_{i+1}, A D e_{j+1}⟩)_{i,j<m} = |γ| · √det(⟨A e_i, A e_j⟩)_{i,j<n} · |det D|. No injectivity of A or invertibility of D is assumed; for m = 0 the left side is √(det of the empty matrix) = 1.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (A : Eucl (m + 1) →L[ℝ] Eucl P) (D : Eucl (m + 1) →L[ℝ] Eucl (m + 1)) (γ : Eucl P), γ ∈ LinearMap.range A.toLinearMap → (∀ y : Eucl (m + 1), inner ℝ γ (A (D y)) = y 0) → Real.sqrt (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin m => inner ℝ (A (D (EuclideanSpace.single i.succ 1))) (A (D (EuclideanSpace.single j.succ 1)))).det = ‖γ‖ * Real.sqrt (Matrix.of fun i j : Fin (m + 1) => inner ℝ (A (EuclideanSpace.single i 1)) (A (EuclideanSpace.single j 1))).det * |D.det|
subproblem.natural_proof:
This is step 4 of the parent proof (the Jacobian identity J_m(A∘D∘ι) = |ĝ|·J_n(A)·|det D|, ι(z) := [0,z]), in Gram-determinant form and without the injectivity of A or the invertibility of D: in degenerate cases both sides vanish. In the parent's application A = DΦ(w), D = Dχ(y), γ = G(Φ(w)), and the left side is J_m of the slice map. We use a Gram-matrix/Cramer computation instead of the block-triangular normDet computation; it proves the same identity and needs no orthonormal bases of subspaces.

Notation. n := m+1, e_i := EuclideanSpace.single i 1 (i < n). v_j := A(D e_j) for j < n. Γ := (⟨v_i, v_j⟩)_{i,j<n} (an n×n real matrix); Γ′ := Γ.submatrix Fin.succ Fin.succ = (⟨v_{i+1}, v_{j+1}⟩)_{i,j<m}, which is exactly the matrix on the left-hand side; G_A := (⟨A e_i, A e_j⟩)_{i,j<n}; [D] is the matrix of D in the standard basis, [D]_{k i} := (D e_i)_k (LinearMap.toMatrix for EuclideanSpace.basisFun), so det [D] = D.det (LinearMap.det_toMatrix).

1. (Dual relation.) For j < n the hypothesis with y := e_j gives ⟨γ, v_j⟩ = (e_j)_0, which is 1 if j = 0 and 0 otherwise.
2. (Γ = [D]ᵀ G_A [D].) Expanding in the standard basis, D e_i = Σ_k [D]_{k i} e_k, so by linearity v_i = Σ_k [D]_{k i} A e_k. Bilinearity of the inner product gives ⟨v_i, v_j⟩ = Σ_k Σ_l [D]_{k i} ⟨A e_k, A e_l⟩ [D]_{l j} = ([D]ᵀ G_A [D])_{i j}. Hence det Γ = det([D])² · det G_A = (D.det)² · det G_A (Matrix.det_mul, Matrix.det_transpose).
3. (Claim: det Γ′ = |γ|² · det Γ.)
(a) Case D.det = 0. Then D is not injective (LinearMap.bot_lt_ker_of_det_eq_zero); pick y ≠ 0 with D y = 0. The hypothesis gives y_0 = ⟨γ, A(D y)⟩ = 0. Put z := (y_1, …, y_m) ∈ ℝ^m (z i := y (i.succ)); z ≠ 0 because y ≠ 0 and y_0 = 0. (For m = 0 this case cannot occur: the hypothesis with y = e_0 gives ⟨γ, A(D e_0)⟩ = 1, so D ≠ 0 and, D being 1×1, D.det ≠ 0.) Since y_0 = 0, y = Σ_{j<m} z_j e_{j+1}, so Σ_j z_j v_{j+1} = A(D y) = 0, and (Γ′ z)_i = ⟨v_{i+1}, Σ_j z_j v_{j+1}⟩ = 0 for every i. So Γ′ has a nonzero kernel vector and det Γ′ = 0 (Matrix.exists_mulVec_eq_zero_iff). By step 2, det Γ = 0, and the claim reads 0 = 0.
(b) Case D.det ≠ 0. Then D is bijective (ContinuousLinearMap.toContinuousLinearEquivOfDetNeZero). As γ ∈ range A, γ = A u₀ for some u₀; let c := D⁻¹ u₀, so γ = A(D c) = Σ_j c_j v_j (expand c = Σ_j c_j e_j). For every i, (Γ c)_i = Σ_j ⟨v_i, v_j⟩ c_j = ⟨v_i, γ⟩ = δ_{i0} by step 1, i.e. Γ *ᵥ c = Pi.single 0 1. Moreover |γ|² = ⟨γ, Σ_j c_j v_j⟩ = Σ_j c_j ⟨γ, v_j⟩ = c_0. Cramer's rule: cramer Γ b = adjugate Γ *ᵥ b and adjugate Γ * Γ = det Γ • 1, so cramer Γ (Γ *ᵥ c) = det Γ • c; evaluating at 0 (Matrix.cramer_apply), det Γ · c_0 = det(Γ.updateCol 0 (Pi.single 0 1)). Expand this determinant along column 0 (Matrix.det_succ_column_zero): column 0 is the vector Pi.single 0 1, so only the row-0 term survives, with sign +1 and minor obtained by deleting row 0 and column 0; that minor is Γ′, because the other columns are those of Γ. Hence det Γ′ = det Γ · c_0 = |γ|² · det Γ.
4. (Combine.) By steps 2 and 3, det Γ′ = |γ|² · (D.det)² · det G_A.
5. (Square roots.) √(det Γ′) = √(|γ|² · (D.det)²) · √(det G_A) (Real.sqrt_mul, the first factor is ≥ 0) = |γ| · |D.det| · √(det G_A) (Real.sqrt_sq for |γ| ≥ 0, Real.sqrt_sq_eq_abs), which is the asserted identity after reordering the factors. No sign condition on det G_A is needed. For m = 0, Γ′ is the empty matrix with determinant 1, and all steps remain valid. ∎
proof_key_steps: Dual relation ⟨γ, A D e_j⟩ = δ_{j0} from the hypothesis.
Gram matrix Γ of v_j = A D e_j equals [D]ᵀ G_A [D], so det Γ = (det D)² det G_A.
If det D = 0: a kernel vector y of D has y_0 = 0, so its tail is a nonzero kernel vector of Γ′ and det Γ′ = 0 = RHS.
If det D ≠ 0: γ = Σ c_j v_j with Γc = e_0 and |γ|² = c_0; Cramer's rule and Laplace expansion along column 0 give det Γ′ = c_0 det Γ.
det Γ′ = |γ|² (det D)² det G_A; take square roots (Real.sqrt_mul, sqrt_sq_eq_abs).

audit.reason: The prose and matrix-determinant proposition agree. The singular-D case supplies a nonzero tail kernel vector; the nonsingular case uses Cramer's identity without assuming the Gram matrix invertible. Square-root factorization is valid, including m = 0. Matrix.of ensures the intended matrix constructions.
